column1: What kind of library is the Teensy Command Server?
column2: A copy-and-extend firmware template. A board dev copies it and registers plain functions as commands/telemetry/hooks; the library owns all networking: TCP, NDJSON framing, schema, telemetry push, e-stop, heartbeat.

column1: What is the one rule for how the controller talks to a board?
column2: The controller only interacts with the board through registered functions. If a capability is not in the schema, it cannot be called.

column1: Do board developers write any networking or JSON code?
column2: No. The library handles TCP, framing, JSON parse/serialize, schema, dispatch, response formatting, telemetry push, e-stop and heartbeat. Devs supply identity, registrations, handlers, telemetry values, and safe-state hooks.

column1: How is the board's schema produced?
column2: It is GENERATED from the same registration metadata used for dispatch (contract 5.3), never hand-written. That prevents the declared schema from drifting from callable behavior.

column1: Name the four source layers and their dependency direction.
column2: support (std lib only) then api (public types) then core (protocol engine) then platform (QNEthernet adapter). A layer may depend only on layers to its left.

column1: What is the critical layering invariant?
column2: src/core and src/api never include QNEthernet or Arduino networking types. All platform I/O lives in src/platform/qnethernet. Time enters core via an injected Clock, I/O via an injected Transport, so core is host-testable.

column1: What is the entire public surface of the library?
column2: src/TeensyCommandServer.h (the facade) plus src/api/*. Everything in src/core and src/platform is a private implementation detail.

column1: Why fixed-capacity with no per-message heap allocation?
column2: The Teensy has no MMU and runs for days; heap fragmentation is a real failure mode (contract 11). All buffers are sized at compile time in src/support/Limits.h.

column1: What does 'schema-first' mean?
column2: The schema is the FIRST message the board sends on every controller connection, unsolicited. It advertises the board's commands, telemetry, and state.

column1: List the wire message types.
column2: schema, command, response, telemetry, event (estop_triggered / estop_ack), and heartbeat.

column1: How is telemetry delivered, and why does it matter?
column2: Unsolicited push about every 50 ms while a session is active; never requested. It IS the liveness signal: if it stops, the controller declares the board lost. It must keep flowing even during e-stop.

column1: What are the only two board response statuses?
column2: Exactly ok and error. Never timeout. New failure modes are contract 17 error codes, never new statuses.

column1: What is the wire framing format?
column2: Newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON): one compact JSON object per line, terminated by a newline.

column1: What does the board do with controller_ts?
column2: Copies it into the response untouched: never interprets, compares, or persists it. It is a controller round-trip token and is not exposed to handlers.

column1: What are the four V1 argument/field value types?
column2: Int (signed 32-bit), Float (finite JSON number; reject NaN/Inf), Bool, String. No nested objects.

column1: List the six contract 17 board error codes.
column2: MISSING_FIELD, INVALID_TYPE, UNKNOWN_COMMAND, INVALID_ARGUMENT, INTERNAL_ERROR, ESTOP_ACTIVE.

column1: Which error codes does the LIBRARY emit before a handler runs?
column2: MISSING_FIELD (declared arg absent), INVALID_TYPE (wrong JSON type), UNKNOWN_COMMAND (no such registered command), and INVALID_ARGUMENT for an undeclared extra argument.

column1: Which error code does the HANDLER own?
column2: INVALID_ARGUMENT for domain failures, e.g. a value outside the hardware-safe range. Structural validation is already done by the library.

column1: Why is there no CommandResult helper for UNKNOWN_COMMAND?
column2: Only the library dispatcher emits it, before any handler runs; a command that reaches a handler is by definition known. So there are five helpers for six codes.

column1: What is the void* context pattern?
column2: Every registration takes a void* context that the library hands back to the callback untouched. It lets a plain function pointer reach board state without name-globals or std::function/heap. Recover it with static_cast to your state type.

column1: Why function pointers instead of std::function?
column2: To avoid heap allocation in the steady-state path. context carries the state, so no captures are needed.

column1: setIdentity(...) — what does it do?
column2: Validates board_id, protocol_version, firmware_version are non-empty, then copies them into fixed library storage. board_id becomes 'source' on every outbound message and is how the controller routes to the board.

column1: registerCommand(spec, handler, context) — what does it do?
column2: Copies the command and arg names into the fixed registry; rejects duplicates (5.2) and over-capacity (16 cmds / 8 args) via a Status; wires handler+context for dispatch; and records the metadata that becomes the schema 'commands' entry (same data as dispatch, 5.3).

column1: What is in a CommandSpec?
column2: name, args (an ArgumentSpec array), arg_count, and blocked_by_estop. blocked_by_estop is explicit and required.

column1: registerTelemetrySchema(fields, count) vs setTelemetryProvider(fn, ctx)?
column2: The first DECLARES the shape (field names and types, into the schema telemetry section). The second SUPPLIES the values (the snapshot function pushed every 50 ms).

column1: setEstopHook / setControllerLossHook — what do they store?
column2: The two SafetyHook function pointers plus context. The e-stop hook runs when an estop message arrives; the loss hook when the controller link drops. Their return value gates the estop_ack.

column1: enableCountersDiagnosticCommand() — what does it do?
column2: Registers a built-in get_counters command exposing the contract 25 counters (dropped frames, oversized lines, over-budget hooks, bytes). It appears in the schema like any command.

column1: What is the registration-to-serve sequence?
column2: construct, setIdentity, setNetworkConfig, registerCommand(s), registerTelemetrySchema, setTelemetryProvider, setEstopHook, setControllerLossHook, start(), then loop { service() }.

column1: What are the four steps of start()?
column2: 1) validate registration completeness; 2) generate the schema and verify it fits 8192 bytes; 3) commitSeal() so the registry becomes immutable; 4) construct the telemetry scheduler and session driver (placement-new, no heap) and open the TCP listener.

column1: What happens if you call register*/set* after start()?
column2: It returns StatusCode::RegistrationSealed. Registration is immutable after start(); there is no dynamic command registration in V1.

column1: What does service() do, and how often is it called?
column2: Called every loop iteration, non-blocking. In one pass it accepts/replaces the session, receives+frames+parses inbound lines, dispatches commands, pushes due telemetry, answers heartbeats, runs safety hooks, and flushes outbound writes under the transmit deadline.

column1: Why must handlers and loop() never block?
column2: service() must keep turning; if it stalls, telemetry stops and the controller declares the board lost. Handlers record intent and return immediately; the loop does timed work.

column1: What is the command handler signature?
column2: api::CommandResult (const api::CommandContext&, api::ObjectWriter& result, void* context). It is a raw function-pointer type (api::CommandHandler).

column1: What has the library already validated before a handler runs?
column2: The command name is registered, all declared args are present, and each arg's JSON type matches; undeclared extra args are rejected. The handler only does domain validation.

column1: What are the handler rules for blocking, networking, and allocation?
column2: Non-blocking (start the action and return), no networking inside the handler, no exceptions across the boundary, and no dynamic allocation.

column1: Who owns board_proc_us?
column2: The library. Handlers must not add it; ObjectWriter silently refuses a field named board_proc_us. The library times the handler and inserts it into the result object.

column1: What are the CommandArgs accessors and their return value?
column2: has(name), and getInt/getFloat/getBool/getString(name, out). Each returns bool, false if the arg is absent or the wrong type.

column1: What is the lifetime of a string obtained from CommandArgs?
column2: Valid ONLY during the current handler call (while the framer line is acquired). Copy out anything you keep; never retain a reference into the parsed document.

column1: What are the ObjectWriter accessors and what does a false return mean?
column2: addInt / addUInt64 / addFloat / addBool / addString(name, value), each returns bool. false means it would not fit the fixed buffer; surface it as INTERNAL_ERROR. The library never sends a truncated line.

column1: Why is ObjectWriter's capacity smaller than the 8 KB line?
column2: Its budget is the 8 KB line minus a reserved envelope (status, result/error structure, board_proc_us, escaping, newline), so a handler can never produce a result the library cannot wrap into a valid response.

column1: What are the CommandResult factories?
column2: ok(); error(code, msg); and helpers missingField / invalidType / invalidArgument / internalError / estopActive. Error messages are copied into a fixed 160-byte buffer with an 'exceeds capacity' fallback.

column1: What is the telemetry provider signature and its rules?
column2: bool (api::ObjectWriter& telemetry, void* context). It must be fast and non-blocking, with no sensor waits or networking. Copy the latest snapshot; return true to send the frame or false to skip it.

column1: How does the library schedule telemetry?
column2: On its own ~50 ms scheduler while a session is active, coalescing delayed periods to the latest snapshot. It is never solicited by a controller request.

column1: What is the SafetyHook signature and the return-value contract?
column2: bool (void* context). Return true ONLY when board-local safe state has actually been applied. estop_ack is sent only after the e-stop hook returns true; on false no ack. Hooks must be idempotent, within about a 100 ms budget.

column1: What is 'honest e-stop'?
column2: The board sends estop_ack with details.state exactly 'safe' only after the e-stop hook confirms safe state (returns true). On failure, no ack. There is no board-side software e-stop latch.

column1: What is blocked_by_estop, and who enforces the gating?
column2: Per-command metadata: true for anything that actuates hardware, false only for diagnostics safe during e-stop. E-stop gating is enforced by the CONTROLLER dispatcher, not the board. If absent, the controller treats it as blocked (fail-safe).

column1: May a board keep its own software e-stop latch?
column2: No. estop_reset is client-to-controller and never sent to boards, so a board latch could never be cleared. A board may reject with ESTOP_ACTIVE only for a live board-local hardware safety condition, never a latched prior estop.

column1: Name the two safety hooks and when each fires.
column2: on_estop_received (e-stop hook) fires on a controller-commanded e-stop; on_controller_lost (controller-loss hook) fires when the telemetry/heartbeat link drops. Same signature; both drive local safe state.

column1: What are the key fixed capacities?
column2: 16 commands max, 8 args per command, 24 telemetry fields, 24 state fields, 1 KB inbound line, 8 KB outbound line. All constexpr in src/support/Limits.h; exceeding fails with CapacityExceeded, never realloc/truncate.

column1: What are the integer rules?
column2: seq is uint64. Contract int is int32 (validate range). float must be finite (reject NaN/Inf as INVALID_ARGUMENT). Durations use unsigned millis()/micros() subtraction so wraparound stays correct.

column1: What is the inbound line-overflow behavior (LineFramer)?
column2: Discard through the next newline, increment the oversized_lines counter, and recover on the next valid line. Never a truncated parse.

column1: What is the outbound overflow behavior?
column2: Never send a truncated line: a response becomes a compact INTERNAL_ERROR; telemetry is dropped and counted (contract 11.2).

column1: What are the two line-length limits and why do they differ?
column2: Controller-to-board is 1 KB (keep command args small and flat); board-to-controller is 8 KB, because the full schema is sent outbound and must fit the controller receive limit.

column1: What are the four verification commands?
column2: python3 tools/check_invariants.py (layering guardrails); python3 tools/check_contract_sync.py (contract hashes); ./tools/run_host_tests.sh (host C++ tests); ./tools/build_teensy.sh (Teensy compile). Hardware tests are manual only.

column1: How is the architecture enforced, not just by convention?
column2: check_invariants.py fails the build if core/api include QNEthernet, if DynamicJsonDocument appears, and similar; contracts are hash-pinned by check_contract_sync.py.

column1: What are the naming conventions?
column2: Types PascalCase; methods/functions camelCase; constants kPascalCase (or UPPER_SNAKE for contract-vocabulary strings); members trailing_underscore_; files PascalCase.h, one concern per pair.

column1: What is the comment-style rule?
column2: Comments state constraints the code cannot show (e.g. a contract ref like '13.6: deadline-bounded'), never narrate the code.

column1: What is the error-handling style across the library boundary?
column2: No C++ exceptions and no RTTI; errors are return values: Status enums for registration/config, CommandResult for handlers.

column1: How does the demo stack find a board?
column2: /demo up (tools/demo_stack.py) scans the subnet for anything answering TCP :5051 with a schema-first frame, then starts Redis, the special-lamp controller, and the dashboard GUI at http://127.0.0.1:8000/.

column1: What makes a board discoverable by the demo stack?
column2: start() opens the :5051 listener and the board sends its schema as the first line on connect, which is exactly what the discovery probe matches.
